title: The Bridge: Blocks to Code
description: Every block you stacked last module has an exact Python equivalent. Once you see the pattern, blocks stop looking like a separate language.

content.value: Take the obstacle-avoidance program from the end of last module — a repeat-forever block containing an if/else. Written as Python, it looks like this:

Line up each piece: repeat forever became while True:. The if/else block became Python's if/else, with the exact same shape — a condition, a then-branch, an else-branch. "Move forward" became a real function call, robot.forward(50), with an actual number for how fast.

The structure — sequence, decision, loop — didn't change at all. What changed is precision: blocks let you say "if wall ahead" in plain words, but code needs an exact, checkable condition, like robot.distance() < 30. That's the real difference between blocks and code: not what you can express, but how exactly you have to say it.

block: "if wall ahead"     -->  code: "if robot.distance() < 30"
block: "move forward"      -->  code: "robot.forward(50)"
block: "repeat forever"    -->  code: "while True:"

Indentation in Python isn't just for readability — it's how Python knows which lines belong inside the loop or the if/else, the same job the visual nesting of blocks was doing. Get the indentation wrong and Python reads the structure wrong too.
Key takeaway: blocks and code express the exact same three shapes — sequence, decision, loop. Code just requires exact conditions and numbers where blocks let you gesture at them in words.

quiz.question: What Python keyword does a 'repeat forever' block translate to?
quiz.explain: An unlimited repeat, with no built-in end, is exactly what `while True:` means in Python.

quiz.question: What's the real difference between an 'if wall ahead' block and `if robot.distance() < 30:` in code?
options: Same idea, but code needs an exact, checkable numeric condition instead of a plain-language phrase
Code can't express conditions at all
quiz.explain: The shape (a decision) is identical — code just demands precision blocks let you skip.

quiz.question: What job does indentation do in Python that visual nesting did for blocks?
options: It tells Python exactly which lines belong inside a loop or if/else — the same job as a block being nested inside another
It controls how fast the program runs
quiz.explain: Indentation is how Python reads structure. Get it wrong, and lines end up inside (or outside) the wrong block entirely.
